IMMIGRATION AND REFUGEE BOARD (APPEAL DIVISION) 
 LA COMMISSION DE L’IMMIGRATION ET DU STATUT DE REFUGIE (SECTION D’APPEL) 
 V99-00227 REASONS FOR DECISION AND ORDER 
 
APPELLANT (S)/A PPLICANTS APPELANT (S)/REQUÉRANT (S) 
JAGJIT SINGH DOGRA 
 
 
 
RESPONDENT INTIMÉ
 THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION 
 
 
 
DATE (S) OF HEARING DATE (S) DE L’A UDITION

 Vancouver, B.C.

CORAM CORAM
 Nirmal Singh 
 
 
 
FOR THE APPELLANT (S)/APPLICANT (S)) POUR L ’APPELANT (S)/REQUÉRANT (S) 
K. O'Connor Coulter Barrister & Solicitor 
 
 
 
FOR THE RESPONDENT POUR L ’INTIMÉ

1999 CanLII 14714 (CA IRB)
 V99-00227 
 
 These are the reasons for the decision in the appeal of XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the "appellant"), filed pursuant to section 77 of the Immigration Act
1 (the “Act ”) from the refusal to approve the sponsored application of his wife, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the principal applicant), his son, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, and his daughter, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, from India. THE REFUSAL
 The sponsored application was refused be cause the applicants were found to be members of the inadmissible class of persons described in paragraph 19(2)(d) of the Act
.2 Specifically, the applicants failed to comply with the requirements of subsection 9(3) of the Act
.3 THE ISSUES
 Counsel for the appellant, at the outset, advised the panel that the appellant does not dispute the validity of the refusal in law. The sole issue to be resolved is whether their exist sufficient compassionate or humanitarian considerations in this case that would warrant the granting of special relief under the Appeal Division's discretionary jurisdiction pursuant to paragraph 77(3)(b) of the Act. THE EVIDENCE
 
 
1 R.S.C. 1985, as amended. 
2 Paragraph 19(2)(d) of the Act reads 19(2)(d): No immigrant and, except as provided in subsection (3), no visitor shall be granted admission if the immigrant or visitor is a member of any of the following classes: (d) persons who cannot or do not fulfil or comply with any of the conditions or requirements of this Act or the regulations or any orders or directions lawfully made or given under this Act or the regulations. 
 3 Subsection 9(3) of the Act states: Every person shall answer truthfully all questions put to that person by a visa officer and shall produce such documentation as may be required by the visa officer for the purpose of establishing that his admission would not be contrary to this Act or the regulations. 
1999 CanLII 14714 (CA IRB)
 - 2 - V99-00227 
 
 The appellant is 43 years old. He was born in India. He and the principal applicant were married on January 18, 1987. Their daughter, XXXXXXXX, and their son, XXXXXX, were born on July 11, 1988 and June 12, 1991, re spectively. Sometime during 1992, the appellant submitted an application for permanent residence in Canada as a single, never married, dependent son of his mother. The appellant's mother had earlier emigrated from India and is a permanent resident of Canada. The appellant's application for permanent residence in Canada was sponsored by his mother. The appellant testified that he does not know whether his mother sponsored him as a single, never married, dependent son or whether she sponsored him as a son who had been married and had a wife and two children. The appellant testified that he sought the help of a lawyer, Mr. XXXXXX, in filling up his application for permanent residence in Canada. Mr. XXXXXX allegedly advised the appellant that he would be denied a Canadian immigrant visa if he declared that he had a wife and children. The appellant testified that on the advice of Mr. XXXXXX, he did not mention his marriage nor his dependent children in his application for permanent residence in Canada. The appellant testified that had he known that he would land in such a difficulty as he faces now, he would not have listened to Mr. XXXXXX's advice and provided false information in his application. Subsequently, a visa officer interviewed the appellant regarding his application for permanent residence in Canada. The appellant testified that he lied to the visa officer and did not disclose his marriage nor the existence of his wife and dependent children. The appellant was issued an immigrant visa as a single, never married, dependent son of his Canadian resident mother. On July 7, 1993, the applicant was landed in Canada. The appellant testified that at the time of his landing, at the port of entry, he was asked about his marital status and if he had any dependents. The appellant allegedly declared himself as a single, never married, dependent of his mother and did not disclose any of his dependents. 
1999 CanLII 14714 (CA IRB)
 - 3 - V99-00227 
 
 Sometime in late 1994, the appellant visited India. During this visit, he allegedly again sought Mr. XXXXXX's advice regarding the appellant's wife and children's emigration to Canada. The appellant testified that Mr. XXXXXX advised the appellant to continue lying to the Canadian Immigration authorities in regard to his marital status and his dependent children. A new scheme, however, was devised to deceive the Canadian Immigration officials. The appellant's wife XXXXXX was to marry the appellant as a widow of a deceased person in India. The appellant, allegedly on the advice of Mr. XXXXXX, registered a marriage to his wife XXXXXX in India. The appellant testified that, in fact, no form of marriage took place at this time. Under cross-examination, however, th e appellant testified that this marriage took place in front of a judge inside a Court. An arbitrary date, November 30, 1994, of the marriage was provided to the Registrar of Marriages, Jalandhar, India. The appellant's wife XXXXXX was declared as a widow. Based on the information provided to the Registrar of Marriage, the appellant and his wife were issued a marriage certificate.
4 Subsequently, the appellant returned to Canada and sought the advice of Mr. XXXXXXXXX of William Macintosh & Associates, a Vancouver law firm. The appellant testified that he told Mr. XXXXXXXXX about his marriage to a widow in India and that he wanted to sponsor her. The appellant allegedly did not inform Mr. XXXXXXXXX of the true nature of his relationship to XXXXXX in regard to his previous marriage to her. Mr. XXXXXXXXX allegedly advised the appellant that it is important in the appellant's culture to have a religious marriage and the appellant should have such a marriage. One year later, in February 1996, the appellant returned to India. During his visit, he and his wife XXXXXX re-married each other in a religious ceremony at a Sikh temple
5 and the wedding ceremony was photographed.
6 
 
4 Record p. 26. 
5 Record p. 27. 
6 Record pp.40-45.

 In March 1996, the appellant returned to Canada. Two months later, on May 15, 1996, the appellant filed an Undertaking of Assistance on behalf of his wife XXXXXX and their two children. The information in the undertaking indicates that the appellant declared his two children being his stepchildren. The appellant admitted that he obtained his landing in Canada by misrepresentation and now he is a Canadian citizen. He sought protection under the Canada Evidence Act. The appellant testified that in the event his wife and children fail to secure their landing in Canada, he would stay in Canada for sometime to earn money and later would return to India. The principal applicant filed her application for permanent residence in Canada on September 18, 1996. The information in her application indicates that she had passed her Matriculation examination and her ability in reading and writing English was well.
7 I n support of her application, the principal applicant provided a death certificate of her alleged first husband, XXXXXXXXXXX.
8 The information in the death certificate indicates that XXXXXXXXXXX died on October 8, 1992. The principal applicant also provided birth certificates of her two children indicating their father's name as Major XXXXX.
9 The appellant testified that he does not know how these certificates were obtained except to say that his wife might know how these certificates were obtained. On March 11, 1997, a visa officer interviewed the principal applicant at New Delhi, India. The principal applicant, during her interview, stated that her first husband XXXXXXXXXXX died in an accident on October 8, 1992. She also told the visa officer that her second husband, the appellant, had wanted her to destroy every document and picture of her first husband, XXXXXXXXXXX, and not to leave any trace of her previous life. She allegedly destroyed all evidence which could have established her relationship to her first husband. 
 
7 Record p. 5. 
8 Record pp. 23-24. 
9 Record pp. 14-19. 
1999 CanLII 14714 (CA IRB)
 - 5 - V99-00227 
 
 Subsequently, the visa office in New Delhi undertook a field investigation in order to establish the appellant's wife's relationship to her alleged first husband XXXXXXXXXXX. XXXXXXXXXXXXX, Counsellor, Immigration Control Officer, at the Canadian High Commission, provides the details of the investigation, in his statutory declaration, dated February 9, 1998.
10 Mr. XXXXXXX met the true widow of Major XXXXX. He also met XXXXXXXXXXXXX mother. They both confirmed Major XXXXX's death. They, however, were unable to identify the appellant's wife nor her two children from their pictures. Later, they visited the neighbourhood where the appellant's wife resided. All the appellant's wife's neighbours were able to identified her as the wife of the appellant and the children being of the appellant. Subsequently, on March 5, 1998,
11 and August 17, 1998,12 the visa officer asked the appellant's wife to undergo DNA testing in order to establish the paternity of her children. There was no response from the appellant's wife. In the meantime, however, the appellant approached his Member of Parliament Honourable XXXXXXXXXXXX's office and asked for assistance regarding the appellant's wife's application for permanent residence in Canada. The Honourable Member of Parliament's office, according to the visa officer’s notes, wrote two letters dated January 21, 1998, and March 6, 1998,
13 to the visa office in New Delhi inquiring about the status of the application of the appellant's wife. The appellant allegedly is a certified welder. He completed a nine month course in welding at a local college. Since April 20, 1998, the appellant has been employed as a welder at FPI International Ltd. 
 
10 Record pp. 66-67. 
11 Record p. 53. 
12 Record p. 51. 
13 Record p. 58. 
1999 CanLII 14714 (CA IRB)
 - 6 - V99-00227 
 
 The appellant has one sister who is a resident of India. His mother and his four other siblings reside in Canada. The visa officer's notes indicate that one of the appellant's sisters was deported from Canada.
14 The appellant's wife, XXXXXX, testified vi a a tele-conference call to India. She allegedly does not know whether the appellant included her and their children in his application for permanent residence in Canada. According to her testimony she did not know, until the appellant's return to India in 1994, that the appellant had lied to the Canadian immigration authorities. Since November 1994, however, she admitted to lying to immigration officials. She testified that it was right thing to do to protect her husband. The idea of her being the widow of someone was hatched at this time. The appellant's wife testified that in 1996, her brother, XXXXXXXX, sought the help of an agent, Mr. XXXXX, to help her in her application for permanent residence in Canada. Mr. XXXXX allegedly fabricated a story in which a deceased person, XXXXXXXXXXX, would be claimed as her first husband. According to her testimony, Mr. XXXXX was able to secure birth certificates for her two children indicating Major XXXXX being their father. He also secured XXXXXXXXXXXXX death certificate. Mr. XXXXX allegedly outlined to the appellant's wife her fictitious marriage to Major XXXXX. It was, however, her brother XXXXXXXX who allegedly coached her, prior to her interview with the visa officer, about the details of the fabricated story regarding her marriage to Major XXXXX. Her brother XXXXXXXX allegedly was deceased in October 1997. XXXXXXXXXXXX, appellant's brother-in-law , testified that he had known the appellant since the appellant's arrival in Canada. Mr. XXXXX allegedly was apprised of true nature of the appellant and his wife's dealings with the Canadian immigration authorities after the visa officer asked for the DNA testing of the appellant's children to establish their paternity. Mr. XXXXX testified that the appellant is honest and hard working. However, the appellant had difficulty in securing jobs due to the appellant's lack of fluency in English. 
 
14 Record p. 57. 
1999 CanLII 14714 (CA IRB)
 - 7 - V99-00227 
 
 ANALYSIS The appellant, during his testimony, portrayed himself to be the victim of bad advice from a lawyer, Mr. XXXXXX, in India. Similarly, the principal applicant first blamed the appellant for keeping her in the dark about his deceiving the Canadian immigration authorities in securing his landing in Canada. Since 1996, she put the blame on the agent, Mr. XXXXX, for concocting a story for her being a widow and blamed her brother for coaching her to tell lies to the visa officer. The appellant had been married for five years and had two children of his marriage when he filed his application for permanent residence in Canada. He, however, lied in his application and declared himself to be single, never married dependent son of his mother.
15 During his interview with the visa officer, the appellant lied about his marital status and the existence of his two dependent children. On March 23, 1993, he signed a solemn declaration in front of a visa officer that the information in his application for permanent residence in Canada is truthful, complete and correct. The appellant also signed item 30 in the application for permanent residence in Canada which in part states: I understand that any false statements or concealment of a material fact may result in my exclusion from Canada, and even though I should be admitted to Canada for permanent residence, a fraudulent entry on this application may be ground for my prosecution and/or removal. The information in the appellant's application for permanent residence in Canada indicates that he passed his Matriculation examination and could read and write English well. It is not credible that he was unaware of the cons equences for providing false information in securing a fraudulent entry to Canada. Nor do I find the appellant's testimony, that he provided false information at the advice of Mr. XXXXXX and would not have done so if he knew the consequences of such misrepresentation, to be credible. 
 
15 Exhibit R-1. 
1999 CanLII 14714 (CA IRB)
 - 8 - V99-00227 
 
 At the time of his landing, the appellant again lied about his marital status and the existence of his two dependent children. The appellant's lies continued. He lied to his previous counsel, Mr. XXXXXXXXX. In 1994, he lied to a Court in India and provided false information about his and his wife's marital status in order to secure a fraudulent marriage certificate. In 1996, he claimed his wife to be a widow and went through a religious marriage with her at a Sikh temple for the sole purpose of deceiving the Canadian immigration authorities. I find it difficult to believe the appellant's testimony that he still does not know whether his mother sponsored him as a single, never married, dependent son or whether she sponsored him as a married son who had a wife and two children. For sometime, since the appellant's arrival in Canada, he has allegedly resided with her mother. It is not credible that he had never discussed this important issue with his mother. Moreover, it is highly unlikely that the visa officer would not confront the principal applicant with the appellant's marriage if indeed, the appellant's mother had sponsored the appellant as her married son. It is more likely than not that the appellant's mother sponsored the appellant as her single, never married dependent son. The appellant's claim of ignorance about how his mother sponsored him is more likely an effort on his behalf to keep his mother out of the conspiracy to which he and his wife have been involved to deceive the Canadian immigration officials. Counsel for the Respondent Minister submitted that the appellant obtained his Canadian citizenship on the basis of the appellant's original deception. In support of his submission, counsel for the Minister relied on section 10(2) of the Citizenship Act
 which reads: 10(2) A person shall be deemed to have obtained citizenship by false representation or fraud or by knowingly concealing material circumstances if the person was lawfully admitted to Canada for permanent residence by false representation or fraud or by knowingly concealing material circumstances and, because of that admission, the person subsequently obtained citizenship. (1974-75-6, c 108,s.9.) 
1999 CanLII 14714 (CA IRB)
 - 9 - V99-00227 
 
 I agree with counsel for the Minister's submis sion that the appellant obtained his Canadian citizenship by either misrepresentation or by concealing material circumstances. In their conspiracy to deceive the Canadian immigration authorities, the appellant and his wife weaved a web of very sophisticated lies. They did not find it reprehensible to use the name of a man killed in an accident as being the husband of the appellant's wife and father of the appellant's children. The appellant, knowing he and his wife had been conspiring to lie in regard to their admission to Canada, approached the office of his Member of Parliament presumably to expedite the processing of his wife's application for permanent residence in Canada. But for the visa officer's insistence that the appellant and his children undergo DNA testing to establish the children's paternity, the appellant and his wife's conspiracy to deceive the Canadian immigration authorities perhaps would never have come to light. The appellant's wife testified that she did not know whether the appellant included her in his application for permanent residence in Canada nor was she aware, until 1994, that the appellant had provided false information to the Canadian immigration authorities in his application for permanent residence in Canada. Either her testimony in this regard is not truthful or in the alternative it reflects on the closeness of their relationship. In a close relationship, a husband would normally discuss whether he is emigrating to Canada alone or whether his wife and children would accompany him. In any event, since 1994, the appellant's wife has been an active particip ant in conspiring to deceive the Canadian immigration authorities. The appellant's wife lied in a Court in India when she declared to be a widow. She lied during her interview with the visa officer. She provided false documents in regard to her children's paternity. The visa office was involved in a lengthy and expensive field investigation. 
1999 CanLII 14714 (CA IRB)
 - 10 - V99-00227 
 
 The appellant's wife testified that it was right to lie to save her husband from any potential prosecution for providing false information. The appellant's wife is a high school graduate and in her application for permanent residence in Canada indicates that she can read and write English well. During her testimony, however, she portrayed herself to be the victim of bad advice from an agent, Mr. XXXXX. She had allegedly not even met Mr. XXXXXX until sometime in 1996. Her marriage in a Court in India took place in 1994 and she declared herself to be a widow. Neither the appellant nor his wife came forward to admit to their lies until the day of the hearing. They were aware that the DNA testing would reveal the true paternity of their children. The potential immigrants' truthfulness in providing information in regard to their applications for permanent residence in Canada is the corner stone of the Canadian immigration policy. Conspiracy to deceive immigration officials brings into dispute the integrity of the entire immigration process. Based on all the evidence, I do not find sufficient compassionate or humanitarian considerations in this case that would warrant the granting of special relief under the Appeal Division's discretionary jurisdiction. The refusal is valid in law. The appeal on behalf of XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, and XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX is dismissed pursuant to subsection 77(4) of the Act
. 
1999 CanLII 14714 (CA IRB)
 - 11 - V99-00227 
 
 ORDER The Appeal Division orders that the appeal be dismissed
 because the refusal to approve the application for landing made by XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, and XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX is in accordance with the law, and there do not exist compassionate or humanitarian considerations that warrant the granting of special relief. “XXXXXXXXXXXX” XXXXXXXXXXXX 
 Dated at Vancouver, B.C. this 13 day of December, 1999. 
You have the right under ss. 82.1(1) of the Immigration Act to apply for a judicial review of this decision, with leave of a judge of the Federal Court - Trial Division. You may wish to consult with counsel immediately as your time for applying for leave is limited under that section.
